title: SubTrack your Grad: Gradient Subspace Tracking for Memory-Efficient LLM Training and Fine-Tuning

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to reduce wall-time and computational cost in memory-efficient LLM training/fine-tuning, specifically avoiding the expensive periodic SVD used by GaLore. Papers [1] and [2] explicitly address the same objective of reducing memory and computational overhead in LLM training by projecting gradients into a low-rank subspace. Both papers highlight the computational inefficiency of periodic SVD updates, which aligns with the stated purpose of this contribution. For example, [1] states: "GaLore relies on time-consuming Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) operations to identify the subspace, and the frequent subspace updates lead to significant training time overhead." This matches the problem-class level objective of reducing wall-time and computational cost in memory-efficient LLM training.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves dynamically updating the gradient's compact subspace via rank-1 updates along Grassmannian-manifold geodesics, leveraging estimation error and the orthogonal complement instead of periodic SVD. Papers [10], [15], and [17] describe Grassmannian rank-one update methods for subspace tracking, which are substantively equivalent to the mechanism here. For example, [10] introduces GROUSE: "an incremental algorithm for identifying a subspace of ℝn from a sequence of vectors in this subspace, where only a subset of components of each vector is revealed at each iteration," and [15] elaborates on GROUSE's use of rank-one updates constrained to the Grassmannian manifold. Similarly, [17] discusses adaptive stochastic gradient descent on the Grassmannian for robust low-rank subspace recovery, which involves rank-one updates constrained to the manifold. These methods align with the underlying primitive of dynamically updating subspaces via Grassmannian geodesics.

### Evaluation
The evaluation design measures wall-time reduction and memory efficiency during LLM training/fine-tuning, using benchmarks like GLUE and SuperGLUE. Papers [1], [2], and [18] use similar evaluation designs. For example, [1] and [2] evaluate memory-efficient LLM training methods using wall-time and memory metrics, while [18] introduces SuperGLUE as a benchmark for general-purpose language understanding systems. The use of GLUE/SuperGLUE benchmarks and wall-time/memory metrics is a standard evaluation design in this domain, making the evaluation facet covered.

### Domain
The domain is memory-efficient LLM training and fine-tuning. Papers [1], [2], [4], [6], [7], [8], [9], and [16] all operate in this application area. For example, [2] states: "Training Large Language Models (LLMs) presents significant memory challenges," and [4] discusses "low-memory LLM training with structured sparse gradients." These papers address memory-efficient optimization techniques for LLM training/fine-tuning, which is the same general application area as this contribution.

## Purpose

The contribution's purpose is to reduce wall-time and computational cost of memory-efficient LLM training/fine-tuning by avoiding the expensive periodic SVD that GaLore uses.

Paper [1] (Q-GaLore) explicitly states: "GaLore relies on time-consuming Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) operations to identify the subspace, and the frequent subspace updates lead to significant training time overhead" — this is exactly the same problem being addressed. Paper [2] (GaLore) introduces the baseline but doesn't address SVD cost. Paper [4] (GRASS) also addresses computational overhead of projection-based methods. Paper [1] is the closest match, directly targeting the SVD overhead in GaLore for memory-efficient LLM training.

## Mechanism

The contribution uses rank-1 updates along Grassmannian-manifold geodesics to dynamically update the gradient subspace, avoiding periodic SVD. Papers [10], [11], [13], [15], [17], [25], [26] all describe Grassmannian rank-one update subspace estimation (GROUSE) — incremental gradient descent on the Grassmannian manifold for subspace tracking via rank-1 updates. Paper [15] explicitly describes "GROUSE... incremental gradient descent on the Grassmannian manifold of subspaces" with rank-one updates. Paper [14] describes "geometric subspace updates" via Riemannian optimization on the Grassmannian. Paper [12] describes "subspace tracking algorithms which utilize the Grassmann manifold" with dynamical models. The core primitive — rank-1 geodesic updates on the Grassmannian to track a subspace without full SVD — is well-established in papers [10], [13], [15]. However, the specific application of this to gradient subspace tracking in LLM training, using estimation error and orthogonal complement, is a combination. The underlying primitive (Grassmannian rank-1 geodesic updates for subspace tracking) is clearly covered by [15] and [10].

## Evaluation

The contribution evaluates on GLUE and SuperGLUE benchmarks, measuring wall-time reduction and memory efficiency. Paper [18] introduces SuperGLUE. Papers [1] and [2] evaluate LLM training/fine-tuning methods with wall-time and memory metrics. The evaluation design — benchmarking on GLUE/SuperGLUE with wall-time and memory measurements for LLM fine-tuning — is the same design used in [1] and [2], which also compare against GaLore with similar metrics. This is a standard benchmark family (GLUE/SuperGLUE) with the same metric semantics (wall-time, memory overhead).

## Domain

The domain is memory-efficient LLM training and fine-tuning. Papers [1], [2], [3], [4], [6], [7], [8], [9], [16] all operate in this exact domain. Paper [2] is the canonical reference for memory-efficient LLM training via gradient projection.

### Purpose
The contribution aims to demonstrate that SubTrack-Grad achieves a favorable accuracy/efficiency trade-off, showing that the speedup does not sacrifice task performance. Papers [1], [6], and [9] all address similar objectives of balancing memory efficiency and task performance in LLM training. For example, [1] states, "reducing trainable parameters and optimizer states without compromising performance," and [6] mentions, "reduces memory usage without compromising performance." The mechanism involves an empirical comparison of SubTrack-Grad against GaLore on GLUE/SuperGLUE fine-tuning and pre-training, measuring downstream performance alongside runtime and memory. Papers [15], [16], [17], and [20] describe subspace tracking algorithms that use gradient-based methods for efficient optimization, which aligns with the underlying primitive of gradient-based subspace tracking used in SubTrack-Grad. For example, [15] discusses "gradient-based adaptive algorithms for subspace tracking," and [16] describes "incremental gradient descent on the Grassmannian manifold of subspaces." These mechanisms are substantively equivalent to the gradient-based subspace tracking primitive in SubTrack-Grad.

The evaluation design measures performance comparable to or better than GaLore with significant runtime reduction and minimal memory overhead. Papers [1], [6], and [9] use similar evaluation designs, comparing memory-efficient methods against baselines like full-rank training or other low-rank approaches, with metrics for runtime, memory usage, and task performance. For instance, [6] evaluates "runtime reduction and performance parity with GaLore," and [9] measures "memory reduction and comparable task accuracy." These evaluation setups match the design-level equivalence rule.

For example, [1] focuses on "memory-efficient LLM training," and [9] discusses "efficient fine-tuning methods integrating weights and gradient low-rank adaptation." ### Purpose
The purpose of the contribution is to explain why subspace tracking helps optimization and provide theoretical grounding. None of the prior papers explicitly establish or report the same empirical relationship between subspace tracking and optimization benefits, nor do they provide a theoretical explanation for this relationship. While many papers discuss subspace tracking in various contexts (e.g., [1], [2], [5], [9]), and some address optimization theory ([7], [19], [26]), none explicitly connect subspace tracking to optimization benefits in the same way.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves analyzing how tracking the gradient subspace reduces abrupt changes in updates (accelerating convergence) and proving that the method matches GaLore's convergence guarantees while allowing more frequent subspace updates via prior knowledge and orthogonal-space errors. Paper [9] (GaLore) provides a convergence guarantee for gradient low-rank projection in memory-efficient LLM training, which aligns with the convergence guarantee aspect of the mechanism. Paper [4] also provides convergence guarantees for subspace-based methods in LLM training. However, neither explicitly analyzes the reduction of abrupt changes in updates as a mechanism for faster convergence, nor do they incorporate prior knowledge and orthogonal-space errors in the same way. Thus, the mechanism is **partially covered** but not fully equivalent.

### Evaluation
The evaluation facet involves qualitative/theoretical analysis: proving convergence-guarantee alignment with GaLore and arguing reduced abrupt subspace shifts as the mechanism for faster convergence. Paper [9] (GaLore) uses a similar evaluation design, proving convergence guarantees for gradient low-rank projection methods. Paper [4] also provides theoretical convergence guarantees for subspace-based methods. Both use similar evaluation designs (analytical proofs of convergence guarantees), even though the specific claims differ. Therefore, the evaluation design is **covered**.

### Domain
The domain is optimization theory for LLM training. Papers [9] and [4] both address optimization methods for LLM training, specifically focusing on memory-efficient techniques. While the specific sub-problems or methods differ, the general application area (optimization theory for LLM training) is the same. Thus, the domain is **covered**.
